clue.text: Black Prince retrospective? Dull pretentious nonsense

indicators.note: a retrospective looks back over the past, so the letters are read looking backwards

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for black, as on pencils
Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare's history plays

explanation.surface: A gallery mounts a retrospective on the Black Prince, and a critic dismisses it as dull, pretentious twaddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Black Prince was Edward III's son, which steers you towards Edward; the prince you need is Shakespeare's Hal, and only he turns round, after B.
explanation.definitionFit: Blah is informal for empty, bombastic talk, and as an adjective it also means boring and lifeless.

clue.text: Jack meets loveless Jo on surer ground? They've made a solemn retraction

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis, a round letter, so being without love means dropping that letter
something ground has been crushed and broken up, so the letters are reduced and reformed

blocks.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, and an AB is an able-bodied seaman
the name with its O, love, taken away
the five letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor teams up with Jo March, now unlucky in love, and feels more confident on land.
explanation.walkthrough: Jo is the March sister of Little Women, part of the puzzle's March theme. 'Jack' is the sailor convention, not a playing card or the lifting tool.
explanation.definitionFit: To abjure is to renounce or recant formally, often under oath, so abjurers are people who have publicly taken back a belief.

clue.text: A 14: The Spanish Ego by Brahms and Liszt

definitions.note: 14 is MARCH; here a military march

indicators.note: Brahms and Liszt is rhyming slang for pissed, meaning drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: the punctuation mark itself, read as its name
el is Spanish for the
taken as written, ready to be mixed
taken as written; it joins the mixed letters

explanation.surface: A title in italics, like a march or concert piece called The Spanish Ego, credited to Brahms and Liszt.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon after '14' is not punctuation but wordplay: you read its name. 'Brahms and Liszt' looks like two composers credited for the piece; it is Cockney rhyming slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Bogey is the famous 1914 British military march by Kenneth Alford, whistled in the film The Bridge on the River Kwai.

clue.text: Fancy short musical with European element

indicators.note: as a verb, to fancy is to imagine freely, and fanciful arrangements are made up rather than given
something short lacks its full length, so the word loses its tail

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Someone takes a liking to a brief stage musical with a continental touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy short musical' reads like a description of a show; 'Fancy' only stirs the letters, and the E for European joins them before the stir.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesium is a soft, reactive alkali metal, atomic number 55, used in atomic clocks; it is a chemical element.

clue.text: Contributor to 20D - dysfunctional wooden character

blocks.note: first meaning: one who nods, supplying the 'Show agreement' part of the clue at 20 down
second meaning: Enid Blyton's wooden toy hero, whose spring-mounted head bobs about uncontrollably

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference sends you to 20 down, where 'Show agreement' clues NOD; a noddy is one who nods. Noddy is the little wooden boy of British children's books, whose head never stops nodding.
explanation.definitionFit: Blyton's toy character is carved from wood with a loose, constantly bobbing head, and a noddy is also anyone given to nodding.

clue.text: In unconvincing manner, lost against the Spanish in 14?

indicators.note: one thing set inside another is held within it, so these letters go into the middle of the next

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for lost in tables of match results
14 is MARCH, and Amy is the youngest March sister in Little Women
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Someone fails to convince, having lost a match against Spain in March.
explanation.walkthrough: '14' looks like the month, but the question mark points to the March family of Little Women; the Spanish article sits inside Amy, after L.
explanation.definitionFit: A lame excuse is a weak, unpersuasive one, so doing something lamely is doing it feebly and without conviction.

clue.text: See 3
Lodge by the sea with Hugo perhaps, after leaving hospital

indicators.note: perhaps hedges that the letters are only one possible arrangement, so a different order is wanted
leaving means departing, so the letter for the hospital walks out of the group

blocks.note: taken as written
the name with its H, hospital, removed

explanation.surface: A seaside lodge where someone called Hugo stays after being discharged from hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lodge by the sea' reads as one holiday place; the definition is only 'Lodge', and the H removed is the map sign for hospital, taken from Hugo.
explanation.definitionFit: A gatehouse is the small building at the entrance to an estate, which in Britain is commonly called a lodge.

clue.text: Bowls out over half of county side

indicators.note: taking a half keeps only part of the word and discards the rest

blocks.note: Yorkshire is an English county and one of its first-class cricket teams

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a bowler dismisses batsmen over after over, accounting for half of a county team.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything here sounds like cricket, and 'over' wants to be an over of six balls; it only links. Yorks is also the usual short form for Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, to york a batsman is to dismiss him with a yorker, a ball pitched right at the feet.

clue.text: The suspect on bail at first in 14?

definitions.note: one of the March family, so a person in it

indicators.note: something suspect is dubious and not to be trusted as it stands, so its order is changed
at first means at the very start, so only the opening letter counts

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be mixed
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A suspect is released on bail early in March.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in 14?' looks like 'in March', a date; the question mark signals the March family of Little Women, of which Beth is the third sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Beth March is one of the four sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel, so she is someone in the March household.

clue.text: A doctor seen in dry cleaners in 14

indicators.note: something seen in a place is inside it, so these letters sit within the next ones

blocks.note: taken as written
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
dusters are cloths that clean without water

explanation.surface: A doctor is spotted at the dry cleaner's in March.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dry cleaners' wants to be the shop; read literally, dusters are cleaners used dry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dam Busters March is Eric Coates's stirring theme from the 1955 film about the wartime bouncing-bomb raid.

clue.text: Significant if Little Women rejected a number of scores

indicators.note: what is rejected is thrown out, so that letter is discarded

blocks.note: weighty means important or significant
a little women is its abbreviation, W

explanation.surface: It would be significant if a novel like Little Women were turned down, having already sold many scores of copies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Women' is set as the book title, tying it to the March theme, but here 'Little' just shrinks 'Women' to W.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so four scores make eighty: the answer is a number counted in scores.

clue.text: Flog heroin? Only a little wee joint

indicators.note: only a little of a word is the smallest taste of it, its opening letter

blocks.note: horse is slang for heroin
the opening letter of the word
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A drug dealer sells heroin and just a small spliff on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flog' looks like British slang for sell, fitting the dealing picture; it is the definition in its sense of beat. 'Joint' wants to be cannabis; it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: To horsewhip someone is to thrash them with a riding whip, so it is a direct synonym for flogging.

clue.text: Some flee Cheshire? They suck!

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters are a portion of the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: People abandon an English county, which apparently is awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They suck!' sounds like slang for being rubbish; read literally, it is what bloodsucking worms do. Cheshire is a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeches are worms that attach to skin and draw blood, so sucking is exactly what they are known for.

clue.text: A river between Central Germany and Switzerland's border

indicators.note: central means at the very middle, so only the letter at the centre is kept
to come between two things is to be enclosed by them on either side

blocks.note: the fourth of seven letters, at the centre
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river on maps
CH is the international code for Switzerland, from Confoederatio Helvetica

explanation.surface: A geography note: a river runs between central Germany and the Swiss frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue sounds like a description of the Rhine; 'border' is the definition, and the A and R slot between M and CH.
explanation.definitionFit: A march is an old word for a frontier region, as in the Welsh Marches along the England-Wales boundary.

clue.text: Dance with Greek goddess outside a bar

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: Hera is queen of the Greek gods
taken as written
to bar is to ban, forbid

explanation.surface: Someone dances with a Greek goddess outside a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' wants to be a pub, and the goddess standing outside it fits; it is the verb meaning prohibit.
explanation.definitionFit: The habanera is a slow Cuban dance in duple time, made famous by the aria in Bizet's Carmen.

clue.text: Prolific 14 scorer (like this American one)

blocks.note: so means in this way
US, the United States
a means one

explanation.surface: Sports talk: a prolific goal-scorer in March, and an American one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scorer' suggests a footballer scoring goals; here it is a composer writing scores of marches.
explanation.definitionFit: John Philip Sousa, the American March King, composed well over a hundred military marches, including The Stars and Stripes Forever.

clue.text: Artist seen in behind first of several wall hangings

indicators.note: to be seen in a place is to be inside it, so these letters sit within the next ones
the first of anything is its opening item, so only the leading letter is used

blocks.note: arse is British slang for the backside
RA, a Royal Academician, is a crossword artist
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An artist appears behind the first of several tapestries in a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' looks like a position word for placing letters after something; it is a noun, the backside, which holds the artist.
explanation.definitionFit: An arras is a rich tapestry hung on walls, named after the French town of Arras where such cloth was woven.

clue.text: Drunken tramp in US showing small wet, round bottom

indicators.note: to come round is to turn about, so the word faces the other way

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
taken as written, to be turned
bum is British slang for the backside

explanation.surface: An American vagrant, the worse for drink, shows a small, damp, rounded backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round bottom' reads as a description of a backside; 'round' belongs to the wet before it, turning it, and the bottom stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewbum is American slang for a habitual drunk living rough; stewed means drunk and a bum is a vagrant.

clue.text: Has arranged a 14 without the final note? That's a pity

indicators.note: arranging puts things in a new order, so the letters are set out differently
going without something means losing it, here the last letter, which is a musical note

blocks.note: the three letters rearranged
Meg, eldest March sister in Little Women, without her last letter G, a musical note

explanation.surface: Someone has arranged a march but left off its last note, which is a pity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a 14' reads as a march to be arranged, as music; it is a March sister, Meg, whose final G is a note.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'what a shame' is the everyday way of expressing regret that something is unfortunate.

clue.text: Second time providing dominant theme ...

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
T is the abbreviation for time
providing means on condition that, if

explanation.surface: Music talk: hearing a passage a second time reveals its main theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second time' reads as a repeat; the two words are separate, a brief moment and the abbreviation T.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring idea or musical figure that runs through a work and gives it its main character.

clue.text: Contents of salads replaced by fruit or asparagus?

indicators.note: replacing means swapping one thing out for another in the same place

blocks.note: the word's first letter, kept
a pear is a fruit, taking the place of the inside letters ALAD
the word's last letter, kept once its inside goes

explanation.surface: A cook asks whether the salad ingredients should be swapped for fruit or for asparagus.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers fruit and asparagus as salad alternatives; actually the inner letters of 'salads' are swapped for a fruit, and the question mark marks asparagus as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Asparagus is sold and served as long green shoots called spears, so the vegetable is an example of them.

clue.text: ... with asymmetry in small part? Show agreement in court

blocks.note: a small part of the word: two letters lifted from inside it
nodding the head shows agreement

explanation.surface: Continuing the music thought: an uneven passage, then a show of agreement in a law court.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis makes this read on from 19 down as one sentence; this clue stands alone. 'court' is the definition, in its church sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A synod is a church council or assembly that can act as an ecclesiastical court, deciding matters of doctrine and discipline.

clue.text: 14 appearing in capital letters

blocks.note: first meaning: a march, Sousa's famous piece of 1889
second meaning: a newspaper, whose letters and news appear in the American capital

explanation.walkthrough: 'capital letters' wants to mean upper case; read it as the capital city and its post, the newspaper published there.
explanation.definitionFit: Sousa wrote a march named after the newspaper, and that paper is the main daily of the United States capital.

clue.text: See 21
Run and hide

blocks.note: first meaning: to move very fast
second meaning: an animal's skin with its fur

explanation.walkthrough: 'Run and hide' reads as advice to flee; both words are nouns or verbs in other senses, one of speed and one of an animal's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelting along is running at full speed, and a pelt is the skin of a fur-bearing animal, which is also called its hide.

clue.text: Roving spider finishes off "dem irksome" flies in 14 (that's always true)

indicators.note: roving means wandering about, so the letters wander from their places
the finish of each word is its end, so the closing letters are taken

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be mixed
the closing letters of the two words
taken as written, ready to be mixed

explanation.surface: A wandering spider complains that the irksome flies are bothering it in March.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flies' looks like the verb and a mixing signal; it is fodder, the insects. The bracket hints at the Latin meaning, always faithful.
explanation.definitionFit: Semper Fidelis is a Sousa march named after the US Marine Corps motto, Latin for always faithful.
